title: Keep another copy
intro: Replication maintains another copy of stored data. In this single-writer example the application writes to the primary.
takeaway: A replica is another data copy. Keeping it updated requires data to travel and be applied.

beats.text: The primary stores application data. The replica holds another copy.
A change is written to the primary. The primary now has revision 8.
The change travels to the replica. The replica must apply it.
The replica reaches revision 8. Both copies now contain the change.

title: A replica can lag
intro: With asynchronous replication, the primary can acknowledge a write while the replica is behind. A read from that replica can return old data.
takeaway: A stale read does not prove the write failed. It tells you which data that particular reader observed.

beats.text: The primary has saved revision 8. The replica is still at revision 7.
The application reads the replica. That query sees the older revision.
Revision 7 comes back successfully. The read is stale, not a failed write.
The primary still holds revision 8. Different copies can answer differently.

title: Check the revision you need
intro: A release assistant needs to verify its own change. It checks the returned application revision rather than treating any successful response as confirmation.
takeaway: In this example, a fresh primary query sees the saved revision. Transaction snapshots and concurrent writers still matter in real systems.

beats.text: The verification expects revision 8. A replica response says revision 7.
Use a fresh read from the primary. Verify against the required revision.
The primary returns revision 8. This matches the saved change.
Match the observation to the decision. A successful query alone is not enough.

title: Received is not applied
intro: PostgreSQL sends write-ahead log records to standbys. Receiving or flushing those records differs from replaying them into query-visible state.
takeaway: What an acknowledgement proves depends on the configured replication mode. Do not equate received bytes with a query seeing the change.

beats.text: The primary sends a change record. The replica receives the record.
Receipt does not mean replay finished. Queries may still observe revision 7.
The replica replays the change. Its query-visible state advances.
Now a fresh query can see revision 8. Check what your acknowledgement means.

title: Failover can lose data
intro: If an asynchronous primary fails before a recent change reaches the standby, promoting that standby can lose the acknowledged change.
takeaway: Replication modes trade latency, availability and durability. This illustrates an asynchronous failure window, not every replication configuration.

beats.text: Async replication: v8 was acknowledged. The standby only has revision 7.
The primary fails before shipping v8. Its newest change is absent elsewhere.
The standby is promoted. It can serve the data it actually has.
Revision 8 is missing after failover. Choose durability requirements explicitly.
